title: "8. From these blocks toward an LDO"
---

[Previous: supply and startup](07-supply-and-startup.qmd) · [Reading route](index.qmd) ·
[Japanese overview](../ja/learning-path.qmd)

The preceding circuits are useful because their limitations can be connected
to a larger job. A low-dropout regulator must compare a sensed output with a
reference, move a pass-device control voltage, and deliver load current while
maintaining accuracy and a controlled response. A good amplifier at one bias
point is only one part of that chain.

This chapter states that chain, makes a few bounded predictions from the saved
OTA observations, and marks the interfaces still unproved. It does not report
a completed LDO or a new OTA optimization campaign.

## Trace a complete correction path

Consider a conceptual PMOS pass device between a positive supply and a regulated
output. The connection below fixes the feedback sign for the positive-gain
OTA of chapter 4. Pass dimensions, divider values and compensation remain to
be designed; this is an application reading view, not an executed netlist.

```text
Supply node: vin_supply
Regulated node: vreg; pass control: ctrl

Ppass(D=vreg, G=ctrl, S=vin_supply, B=vin_supply) W/L = to be designed
Load(vreg -> 0); Cout(vreg, 0)
Rtop(vreg, sense); Rbottom(sense, 0)

Finite error-amplifier inputs:
  positive input = sense
  negative input = reference
  output        = ctrl
Reference and amplifier bias have explicit supply/current dependencies.
```

If load current increases, Cout initially supplies the difference and `vreg`
falls. The sensed voltage falls relative to the reference. For the OTA's
positive differential transconductance, its output `ctrl` falls. This increases
the PMOS pass device's source-to-gate voltage and hence its supplied current,
bringing `vreg` back up. Conversely, a high sensed output raises `ctrl`, weakens
the pass device and reduces delivered current. Reversing the amplifier inputs
would reverse this correction sign for this PMOS connection.

With an unloaded ideal divider, $V_{sense}=kV_{reg}$ where
$k=R_{bottom}/(R_{top}+R_{bottom})$. An ideal infinite-gain equilibrium suggests
$V_{reg}=V_{ref}/k$. Real input current loads the divider; amplifier offset and
finite gain require a nonzero input difference; reference error moves the target;
the pass device requires finite voltage and current to serve the load. These
are separate accuracy paths, not one generic “loop gain” number.

At the regulated output,

$$C_{out}\frac{dV_{reg}}{dt}=I_{pass}-I_{load}-I_{divider}.$$

For a brief load-current increase $\Delta I$ before pass current responds,
the first capacitor-only estimate is
$\Delta V_{reg}\approx-\Delta I\Delta t/C_{out}$. ESR, parasitics, voltage-
dependent capacitance, current limits and subsequent loop response change
that prediction. The equation shows why amplifier bandwidth alone does not
specify a load-step excursion.

## The amplifier output must suit the receiving port

The next circuit receives a voltage and charge, not an abstract voltage gain.
For a PMOS pass device, the required `ctrl` voltage depends on its source
voltage, geometry, load current and allowed source-to-drain drop. Near dropout,
the pass device may have insufficient voltage to supply the load even when
the amplifier drives as hard as it can. The error amplifier cannot correct
missing headroom by increasing its own gain indefinitely.

The pass gate also has voltage-dependent stored charge. The amplifier must
deliver or remove that charge along the actual control trajectory, while
driving parasitic capacitance and any compensation network. A steady-state
MOS gate's small leakage does not imply a small dynamic current requirement.
The sequencing chapter already showed that even an apparently MOS-only input
can draw charging peaks far above its stationary current.

For a simple fixed diagnostic capacitor, $\Delta Q=C\Delta V$. A 5-pF load
moving 0.1 V needs 0.5 pC. If a constant 10-µA net current were available,
the charge-only estimate would be 50 ns. Those are arithmetic scales, not a
prediction of D1's measured settling: current changes with input difference
and output voltage, and the final accuracy band must also be reached.

The saved initial-D1 buffer takes roughly 175–180 ns to enter its stated 1%
band for the 0.25↔0.35-V input steps into 1 MΩ ∥ 5 pF. Its charge balance is
checked from terminal currents. The C diagnostic shows available current near
±11.7 µA only at an output clamped to 0.3 V and a large differential drive.
Neither result establishes that this current remains available near a rail or
through a real pass gate's nonlinear charge trajectory.

No 25-pF initial-D1 result is claimed. The later archive's selected-D1 load
transfer belongs to a different selection history. Keeping the actual
inventory and receiving port visible is more useful than silently borrowing
that result to make the application appear complete.

## What the present evidence supports

| Interface or decision | Evidence available in this edition | What remains to be demonstrated |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Input comparison | A/B current steering; finite-tail common-mode dependence; C's PMOS-input sign at 0.3 V. | Reference/sense voltage ranges over the intended regulator supply and temperature domain. |
| Low-voltage buffer accuracy | Initial D1: source 0.25–0.35 V, output 0.249311–0.347634 V, worst error 2.366 mV. | Required regulator accuracy after reference, divider loading and pass-device operating point are included. |
| Amplifier resource cost | Same six-device initial core, 5.2 µm² drawn MOS area; at most 16.085 µA VDD current on its saved input grid. | Total regulator budget, including reference, divider, startup, compensation and any driver stage. |
| Receiving-port charge | Initial-D1 1-MΩ/5-pF step and C's clamped current sweep, with original circuit identities. | Actual gate-voltage trajectory, nonlinear gate charge, required delivery/absorption, saturation and recovery. |
| Supply and sequencing | Published A75/R75/F75L driven/clamped source histories and current peaks. | Floating pins, current-limited sources, arbitrary stored charge and startup of the integrated regulator. |
| Dynamics and stability | Particular closed-loop signal/step observations under their stated loads. | Regulator return ratio, all relevant crossings, compensation and load/input transients across the chosen domain. |
| Statistical accuracy | Original finite Local source-transfer studies and labeled synthetic resistor scenarios. | A justified combined device/passive/spatial/reference model, layout/PEX effects and silicon validation. |

The [exact C](../studies/learning-path-v1/circuits/C-area-base.cir) and
[initial-D1](../studies/learning-path-v1/circuits/D1-initial-14u.cir) inputs,
[selected observations](../studies/learning-path-v1/summary.json) and
[public reproduction](../studies/learning-path-v1/reproduce.qmd) support the
bounded OTA entries. The table describes measured scope, not a list of items
that can be assumed to pass by choosing a conventional schematic.

## Choose the next design question from the interface gap

A useful next assignment would specify a receiving device and its voltage,
current and charge needs before choosing the amplifier. It could compare a
few fixed nominal control points and a declared trajectory, with a finite
stopping rule and preserved physical inputs. If the necessary trajectory
extends outside this OTA's demonstrated range, a different input polarity,
output stage or bias allocation may be required. That is a new design question,
not a reason to stretch the present claims.

Another question is whether the reference-origin supply path dominates the
eventual error budget. If it does, the unfinished self-bias prototype would
first need its saved equality-check failure diagnosed on its own terms. Its
startup and temperature behavior cannot be inferred from the completed
amplifier sequencing study. A third question is how much passive absolute
accuracy and ratio tracking the sense network actually needs. The synthetic
scenarios teach how to ask that question; they do not provide foundry statistics.

The route has now connected local device behavior to a system decision:
solve current balance, identify the useful signal and unwanted paths, count
the finite bias/input/load resources, and check the required voltage and charge
trajectory. Preserve a failed physical requirement as a result; preserve an
unresolved comparison as unresolved. That discipline makes the next circuit
choice reviewable instead of treating a familiar topology as proof.

For a broader regulator discussion, see
[Wulff's voltage-regulation material](https://analogicus.com/aic2026/voltage_regulation).
